content_voiceover: Let's talk about daratumumab and other anti-CD38 drugs, and why they complicate the blood bank workup. Red cells express CD38, so the drug binds red cells directly and interferes with pretransfusion testing. ABO typing is unaffected. Minor antigen typing may be interfered with. The traditional antiglobulin antibody screen shows a weak pan-reactive positive across every panel cell, which can mask a real alloantibody underneath. The direct antiglobulin test can be positive or negative, inconsistently. But the manual polybrene method for antibody screening is not affected. So the recommended workup is, before starting the drug, get a baseline direct and indirect Coombs test plus minor antigen phenotyping. During treatment, treat screening and panel cells with DTT, dithiothreitol, since CD38 has five disulfide bonds that DTT can break, eliminating interference. Or simply use manual polybrene for crossmatching. And practically, the blood bank should flag these patients in the system so testing isn't unnecessarily delayed.
keypoints: Daratumumab binds CD38 on red cells, causing pan-reactive false-positive antibody screens
ABO typing is unaffected; minor antigen typing and AHG-based screens are interfered with
DTT breaks CD38's five disulfide bonds, removing the interference
Manual polybrene method bypasses the interference entirely
Get baseline Coombs test and minor phenotype before starting therapy
keypoint_voiceover: High-yield point, anti-CD38 drugs like daratumumab bind red cell CD38 and cause a weak pan-reactive antibody screen that mimics a panagglutinin. ABO typing stays reliable, but AHG-based screens and minor typing are affected. The fix is DTT, which breaks CD38's disulfide bonds, or simply using the manual polybrene method, which isn't affected. Always get baseline Coombs testing and phenotype before starting the drug.
